THE DAY'S ROUTINE FOR A SAVOY STUDENT

Classroom work in Savoy College went forward with earnestness and in a mood of seriousness characteristic of the dignity of professors imbued, no doubt, in the spirit of the times. Among those characteristics of Savoy College were those who kept the motto "Keep quiet back there, boys" and for the time being Bill would release his string, and in a few minutes he would commence again, to the amusement of the teacher. News items told of frequent visits of the business manager to notify delinquent subscribers. About the time he reached the College, or even a young lady, rode horseback, the latter picturesquely perched on a side-saddle, and wearing a long, black, bundlesome riding skirt, which of course was taken off before she went into the schoolroom. (A stile block, to assist young ladies in dismounting and mounting, stood on the edge of the campus.)

Again, the student may have ridden to school in a horse-drawn buggy or phaeton. In either case, there was a horse to be unsaddled or unharnessed and tied to a tree in the woods bordering the campus. At noon there was the horse to be fed and watered before the student could eat his own lunch; and in the afternoon there was the matter of saddling or harnessing the animal for the homeward ride.

Life in the bachelor halls had its own separate routine, of course. The following poem by an early student may serve to complete this description and indicate the nature of undergraduate literary efforts of the early Savoy days.
